notes: Switzerland is governed by the four-party 'magic formula' Federal Council (FDP 2, KCVP 2, SP 2, BGB 1); Hans-Peter Tschudi (SP) is President of the Confederation for 1970, so the SP holds ruling slot 3. No Council party fits coalition slot 18, which holds the SP-allied Swiss Federation of Trade Unions. KCVP kept in MD's CVP slot 14 (CVP name from 1971.1.1, renamed during 1970); BGB moved from MD's SVP slot 20 (no popularity) to slot 1, SVP period from 1971.9.22; FDP moved from MD slot 16 to 2 with its MD sprite; PdA in MD slot 19; LdU in 16; National Action in 20. The small Liberal Party (LPS) is not placed.

0.name: Bundespolizei
0.text:
The Federal Police is the political police of the Office of the Federal Prosecutor in Bern and the core of Swiss state security. Together with the political sections of the cantonal police forces, its inspectors keep files on communists, foreign workers, pacifists, students, Third World activists and journalists, tap telephones and shadow the diplomats of the Eastern bloc in Bern and at the United Nations in Geneva.

Its officials regard Switzerland as a front-line state in the Cold War, armed neutrality notwithstanding, and quietly exchange information with Western services. Faced with subversion, they would favour emergency powers, the internment of agitators and an open alignment with the Atlantic camp. Their leverage lies in secrecy, their files and the trust of conservative ministers.

1.name: Bauern-, Gewerbe- und Bürgerpartei
1.text:
The Farmers, Artisans and Citizens' Party grew out of the farmers' parties founded in Zurich in 1917 and in Bern in 1918, whose leader Rudolf Minger became the first agrarian Federal Councillor in 1929. Strongest in Bern, Zurich, Thurgau and Vaud, it won 11 percent in 1967 and holds one seat in the federal government, filled since 1966 by Rudolf Gnägi, head of the Military Department and Vice-President for 1970.

The BGB stands for protected agriculture, the trades and small business, a strong militia army, federalism and strict neutrality, and it is firmly anti-communist. It is exploring a merger with the Democratic parties of Glarus and Graubünden to broaden its base. Its leverage lies in the farmers' and trades associations and in rural Protestant Switzerland.
1.wiki: Party of Farmers, Traders and Independents

1.name: Schweizerische Volkspartei
1.text:
The Swiss People's Party was formed in September 1971 when the Farmers, Artisans and Citizens' Party merged with the Democratic parties of Glarus and Graubünden, which brought in a more urban and social-reformist wing. It keeps the BGB's seat on the Federal Council, held by Rudolf Gnägi, and its strongholds in Bern, Zurich and the rural Protestant cantons.

The party stands for agriculture, the trades and small business, a strong militia army, federalism and strict neutrality, and remains firmly anti-communist. It presents itself as a broad people's party of the middle classes, but its farmers still set the tone. Its leverage lies in the agrarian and trades associations and its pivotal place in the four-party government.

2.name: Freisinnig-Demokratische Partei der Schweiz
2.text:
The Free Democratic Party is the heir of the Radicals who created the Swiss federal state in 1848 and governed it alone for decades; organised nationally since 1894, it remains the party of the establishment. It won 23.2 percent in 1967 and holds two seats on the Federal Council, with Nello Celio at the Finance Department and Ernst Brugger, who takes over the Department of Economic Affairs on 1 January 1970.

The Radicals defend free enterprise, the federal state, a strong army and Switzerland's place in the Western economic order through EFTA, while guarding neutrality. Their base lies among business owners, the Protestant urban middle classes, the professions and the officer corps. Their leverage lies in close ties to the Vorort of industry, the banks and the cantonal governments.

3.name: Sozialdemokratische Partei der Schweiz
3.text:
The Social Democratic Party of Switzerland, founded in 1888, became the strongest party by votes with 23.5 percent in 1967, and since 1959 it has held two seats in the 'magic formula' government. Hans-Peter Tschudi, the energetic head of the Interior Department behind the expansion of old-age pensions, serves as President of the Confederation in 1970, and Pierre Graber is about to succeed Willy Spühler at the Political Department.

The party fights for better pensions, affordable housing, fairer taxation and the democratisation of the economy, while defending neutrality and calling for more development aid. Critical of the Vietnam War but firmly anti-communist, it rests on the trade unions, the industrial towns and the French-speaking cantons. Its leverage lies in the Federal Council and the referendum.

4.name: Die Moskautreuen
4.text:
The Moscow Loyalists are the old guard of Swiss communism: veterans of the Communist Party banned in 1940, of the International Brigades in Spain and of the Comintern years, who still regard the Soviet Union as the fatherland of socialism. They are concentrated in the Basel, Zurich and Geneva sections of the Party of Labour and in its friendship and peace committees.

They defend every turn of Soviet policy, including the Warsaw Pact intervention in Czechoslovakia, distrust the party's talk of a Swiss road to socialism and despise the Trotskyist and Maoist students. They want nationalisation, friendship with the socialist camp and an end to the surveillance of the left. Their leverage lies in party discipline and their ties to the Eastern embassies in Bern.

5.name: Ligue marxiste révolutionnaire
5.text:
The Revolutionary Marxist League was founded in 1969 by young militants in Lausanne who broke with the Party of Labour's youth organisation after the upheavals of 1968, and it is winning recruits among student radicals in Geneva, Zurich and Basel. Led by Charles-André Udry, it aligns itself with Ernest Mandel's Fourth International and publishes in French and German.

The League calls for workers' control, rank-and-file committees against the labour peace agreements, solidarity with Vietnam and the defence of Italian and Spanish workers against the Schwarzenbach initiative. It rejects both Soviet bureaucracy and Swiss social partnership. Its leverage lies on the campuses, in the youth scene and among a minority of immigrant workers.

6.name: Réseau Genoud
6.text:
The Genoud Network centres on François Genoud, a Lausanne financier and lifelong admirer of Hitler who co-founded the Arab Commercial Bank in Geneva in 1958 and managed funds for the Algerian FLN during its war of independence. He owns the literary rights to the writings of Goebbels and Martin Bormann, keeps in touch with Nazi exiles in Cairo and Damascus, and in 1969 paid for the defence of the Palestinian commandos tried in Winterthur for attacking an El Al airliner at Kloten.

The network hates the United States, Israel and liberal capitalism more than it fears Moscow, and backs Arab nationalist regimes and the Palestinian fedayeen. Its leverage lies in money, lawyers, Swiss banking discretion and contacts reaching from Algiers to Damascus.

7.name: Wozchod Handelsbank
7.text:
Wozchod Handelsbank was opened in Zurich in 1966 by the Soviet state banking system to give Moscow a foothold in the West's most discreet financial centre. It handles part of the Soviet Union's sales of gold and precious metals on the Zurich market, finances orders for Swiss machine tools, turbines and watches, and channels hard currency for Soviet foreign trade organisations.

Its managers answer to Moscow, and around the bank gathers a circle of Swiss traders, lawyers and industrialists who profit from commerce with the Eastern bloc. They want neutrality interpreted to Moscow's advantage, starting with an end to the secret 1951 arrangement under which Switzerland follows Western export controls. Its leverage lies in credit, lucrative contracts and gold flows the big banks are eager to handle.

8.name: Aga Khan Foundation
8.text:
The Aga Khan Foundation was established in Geneva in 1967 by Prince Karim Aga Khan IV, the Harvard-educated forty-ninth hereditary imam of the Shia Ismaili Muslims since 1957. His uncle Prince Sadruddin Aga Khan, UN High Commissioner for Refugees since 1966, lives at Bellerive on Lake Geneva, making the city a centre of the Ismaili leadership's diplomacy and charitable work.

The Foundation funds schools, hospitals and rural development for Ismaili and neighbouring communities in East Africa, Pakistan and India, embodying a modernist Shia Islam that values education, enterprise and the participation of women. Wary of revolution and close to Western institutions, it seeks the gradual reform of Muslim societies. Its leverage lies in wealth, organisation and international prestige.

9.name: Anjoman-e Eslami-ye Daneshjuyan
9.text:
The Islamic Students' Association is a small circle of devout Iranian students at the Federal Institute of Technology in Zurich and the universities of Lausanne and Geneva, who meet apart from the leftist Confederation of Iranian Students. They copy the declarations of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled in Najaf since 1965, and send tapes and leaflets home through relatives and pilgrims.

They want the Shah's monarchy replaced by an Islamic order under the guidance of the clergy, denounce his alliance with the United States and Israel and reject communism as godless. Watched by informers of the SAVAK secret police, they have little weight in Switzerland itself. Their leverage lies in their links to the clerical opposition in Qom and Najaf.

10.name: Comité de la Mosquée de Genève
10.text:
The Geneva Mosque Committee gathers Muslim diplomats accredited to the United Nations and to Bern, above all from Saudi Arabia, Morocco, Jordan and Kuwait, together with Arab bankers and merchants settled on Lake Geneva. Switzerland's roughly sixteen thousand Muslims, many of them Turkish and Yugoslav workers, have no purpose-built mosque except the Ahmadiyya mosque in Zurich, and the committee looks to King Faisal to pay for one in Geneva.

It stands for official, conservative Sunni Islam loyal to the Muslim monarchies, keeps its distance from Brotherhood exiles and revolutionaries alike, and values discretion with the Swiss authorities. Its leverage lies in diplomatic status, Gulf money and the banks that manage it.

11.name: Shabab al-Tahrir
11.text:
The Youth of the Tahrir are a handful of Jordanian, Palestinian and Syrian students in Geneva, Lausanne and Zurich who distribute the pamphlets of Hizb ut-Tahrir, the party founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by the judge Taqiuddin al-Nabhani. Banned across the Arab world for courting army officers, the party uses European university towns to recruit quietly among Muslim students.

They call for the restoration of the caliphate, the unification of all Muslim lands under Islamic law and the rejection of nationalism, democracy and both Cold War blocs. In Switzerland they avoid violence and keep clear of the police. Their leverage lies in the fervour of a few students who will carry the message home to Amman, Nablus and Damascus.

12.name: Centre Islamique de Genève
12.text:
The Islamic Centre of Geneva was founded in 1961 by Said Ramadan, the Egyptian son-in-law of Hassan al-Banna and the most prominent Muslim Brotherhood exile in Europe since Nasser's crackdown of 1954. From its premises in the Eaux-Vives quarter he publishes the review Al-Muslimun, receives Arab students and exiles and keeps in touch with Brotherhood networks across Europe and the Middle East. In 1962 he helped found the Muslim World League in Mecca.

The Centre preaches the Brotherhood's vision of Islam as a complete social and political order and rejects Nasserism, Ba'athism and communism alike. Its leverage lies in the prestige of al-Banna's family, contacts with Gulf donors and its role as a meeting point for Islamists in exile.

13.name: Geistige Landesverteidigung
13.text:
Spiritual National Defence was the creed of the 1930s and the war years, when Federal Councillor Philipp Etter rallied the country against Nazism and fascism. Its heirs in the federal administration, civil defence and the officer corps now see the student revolt and the New Left as communist subversion. In 1969 the Department of Justice and Police under Ludwig von Moos sent the red Civil Defence book, written by Albert Bachmann and the historian Georges Grosjean, to every household.

They want strict neutrality, total defence and an emergency regime that would suspend party quarrels, police the universities and expel foreign agitators. Their leverage lies in the bureaucracy, the militia army and a public that still remembers the Alpine Réduit of the Second World War.

14.name: Konservativ-Christlichsoziale Volkspartei der Schweiz
14.text:
The Conservative Christian-Social People's Party is the party of Swiss political Catholicism, heir to the Catholic conservatives of the Sonderbund cantons, organised nationally in 1912 and renamed in 1957. With 22.1 percent in 1967 it holds two Federal Council seats, Ludwig von Moos at Justice and Police and Roger Bonvin at Transport and Energy, and since 1968 it has been chaired by Franz Josef Kurmann of Lucerne.

Rooted in central Switzerland, Fribourg, Valais, Ticino and St. Gallen, it combines Catholic social teaching, family policy and federalism with a Christian-social workers' wing. Neutral, anti-communist and wary of centralisation, it is debating a Christian Democratic name to reach Protestant voters. Its leverage lies in the Catholic associations, the Christian trade unions and the parishes.
14.wiki: Christian Democratic People's Party of Switzerland

14.name: Christlichdemokratische Volkspartei der Schweiz
14.english: Christian Democratic People's Party of Switzerland
14.text:
The Christian Democratic People's Party is the name adopted in 1970 by the Conservative Christian-Social People's Party, the party of Swiss political Catholicism. Chaired by Franz Josef Kurmann, it holds two Federal Council seats and remains strongest in central Switzerland, Fribourg, Valais, Ticino and St. Gallen, while hoping that the label of Christian democracy will win Protestant and urban voters.

The party combines Catholic social teaching, family policy and federalism with a Christian-social workers' wing and a business wing, and seeks a dynamic centre between the Radicals and the Social Democrats. Neutral and anti-communist, it favours a cautious opening toward Europe. Its leverage lies in the Catholic associations, the Christian trade unions and its pivotal place in the government.
14.wiki: Christian Democratic People's Party of Switzerland

15.name: Schweizerische Bankiervereinigung
15.text:
The Swiss Bankers Association was founded in Basel in 1912 and speaks for the big three banks, Union Bank of Switzerland, Swiss Bank Corporation and Swiss Credit Bank, as well as the private banks of Geneva and Basel. Its chairman since 1965 is the Basel private banker Alfred E. Sarasin. The financial centre is booming on flight capital, the Zurich gold market and the Eurodollar trade.

The association defends banking secrecy, anchored in law since 1934, a hard franc and minimal state interference, and resists foreign demands for disclosure. Together with the Vorort of industry and commerce and its Radical allies it shapes economic policy. Its leverage lies in the trust of foreign depositors and its enormous weight in a small economy.

16.name: Landesring der Unabhängigen
16.text:
The Independent Alliance was founded in 1936 by Gottlieb Duttweiler, creator of the Migros retail cooperative, as a movement of consumers against cartels and established party machines. Since Duttweiler's death in 1962 it has remained the political arm of the Migros world, and in 1967 it won 9.1 percent, its best result, with strongholds in Zurich, Bern, Aargau and St. Gallen and its own daily, Die Tat.

The Alliance stands for free competition, low prices, consumer protection and 'social capital', the idea that business owes part of its profits to the community and to culture. It attacks agricultural and industrial cartels as fiercely as state planning and keeps aloof from the governing coalition. Its leverage lies in the Migros network of cooperative members.

17.name: Schweizerischer Bund für Naturschutz
17.english: Swiss League for the Protection of Nature
17.text:
The Swiss League for the Protection of Nature was founded in 1909 to finance the Swiss National Park in the Engadine, opened in 1914, and has grown into the country's largest conservation organisation. In European Conservation Year 1970 it joins the Heritage Society, the young WWF section and the Rheinaubund in campaigns against polluted lakes and rivers, motorways through scenic landscapes and new hydroelectric dams.

The League wants the constitutional article on nature and heritage protection adopted in 1962 enforced, stricter water protection and limits on unchecked growth. It stands outside party politics and the blocs. Its leverage lies in a broad middle-class membership, its scientists and the citizens' initiative and referendum.

18.name: Schweizerischer Gewerkschaftsbund
18.text:
The Swiss Federation of Trade Unions, founded in 1880, unites more than 400,000 members in the metalworkers', construction, railway, public-service and other unions and is closely tied to the Social Democrats. Since the engineering industry's Peace Agreement of 1937 it has traded the strike weapon for collective bargaining, and its leaders sit on federal commissions alongside the employers.

The Federation fights for higher old-age pensions, a shorter working week, rent control and better protection for workers, while its leaders worry that cheap foreign labour weakens their bargaining power. It is anti-communist and attached to labour peace, but its younger members press for a more combative line. Its leverage lies in its membership, its weight inside the Social Democratic Party and the referendum.

19.name: Partei der Arbeit der Schweiz
19.text:
The Swiss Party of Labour was founded in 1944 to succeed the Communist Party banned in 1940, and briefly won strong support in Geneva, Vaud and Basel after the war. Today it polls about 3 percent, holds five National Council seats and has its base in French-speaking Switzerland, where it is led by figures such as Jean Vincent in Geneva and André Muret in Vaud. The federal political police watch its members closely.

Shaken by the Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia, the party stresses a Swiss road to socialism through direct democracy, campaigning for a people's pension, rent control and the nationalisation of key industries. It opposes nuclear armament and the Vietnam War. Its leverage lies among workers in Geneva and Lausanne and in its paper Voix ouvrière.

20.name: Nationale Aktion gegen die Überfremdung von Volk und Heimat
20.english: National Action against Foreign Domination of People and Homeland
20.native_full: Nationale Aktion gegen die Überfremdung von Volk und Heimat
20.text:
National Action was founded in 1961 to fight what it calls the foreign infiltration of Switzerland, as the number of Italian, Spanish and other foreign residents approaches one million. Its best-known figure is James Schwarzenbach, a Zurich publisher from a silk dynasty and its only National Councillor since 1967, whose popular initiative to cap the foreign population at ten percent per canton goes to the vote in 1970.

National Action demands the repatriation of foreign workers, protection of Swiss jobs and housing and the defence of Swiss identity against cosmopolitan elites. Neutralist and anti-communist, it distrusts big business and the governing parties alike. Its leverage lies in resentful small towns and working-class districts that feel ignored by the establishment.

21.name: Nouvel Ordre Européen
21.text:
The New European Order was founded in Zurich in 1951 by veterans of the European fascist movements who found the European Social Movement too moderate. Its secretary-general is the Lausanne teacher Gaston-Armand Amaudruz, who publishes the bulletin Courrier du Continent and coordinates a small international of neo-fascist and racialist groups from his Swiss base.

The Order preaches European racial nationalism, denies the crimes of National Socialism and rejects both American capitalism and Soviet communism. It wants a corporatist, ethnically defined Europe and is hostile to immigration and Zionism. In Switzerland it has only a handful of followers, but its leverage lies in its role as a meeting point for the far right across Europe.

22.name: Schweizer Armee
22.text:
The Swiss Army is a militia in which nearly every Swiss man serves from the age of twenty into his fifties, able to mobilise some 600,000 soldiers within two days. In peacetime it has no general; the Federal Military Department under Rudolf Gnägi and the Chief of the General Staff run it, while the officers' societies carry great weight in business and politics. In November 1969 Switzerland signed the Non-Proliferation Treaty, putting the plans for Swiss nuclear weapons on ice.

The officer corps defends armed neutrality, total defence and modern equipment, still smarting from the Mirage fighter cost scandal of 1964. Should civil order collapse, it would be the decisive power. Its leverage lies in the militia's place in everyday Swiss life.

23.name: Haus Habsburg
23.text:
The House of Habsburg takes its name from the Habsburg castle its ancestors built in the Aargau in the eleventh century, and it was against Habsburg bailiffs that the first Confederates swore their alliance. Seven centuries later Empress Zita, widow of Emperor Charles, the last ruler of Austria-Hungary, has lived since 1962 in a religious home at Zizers in Graubünden, while her son Otto von Habsburg, head of the house, campaigns for European unity from Bavaria.

A handful of Catholic conservatives and romantic legitimists see the dynasty as a symbol of Christian Europe, order and supranational federation against communism. In republican Switzerland its appeal is sentimental rather than political. Its leverage lies in the prestige of the name and in Catholic aristocratic circles.
